newsitem.title: LAOS: Floods hit rice supplies in Laos.
newsitem.headline: Floods hit rice supplies in Laos.

text.p: The worst flooding in memory last year has severely affected Laos' rice supply for 1997, and aid agencies are preparing to help meet the deficit, officials said on Tuesday.
The U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) and the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) have predicted a deficit of 154,000 tonnes this year, even after 25,000 tonnes in anticipated commercial imports.
"Production of rice, the main staple will be insufficient in the coming year. In terms of food availability, 1997 will be much worse than any recent year," said a joint report from the agencies.
It noted that the government, with no significant tax base and no rice stocks of its own, would be hard-pressed to meet the food deficit.
A government spokesman confirmed the situation was bleak but declined to comment further.
At least 43,000 tonnes of sticky rice -- the type of rice eaten in Laos -- would be needed in emergency assistance, said Stephen Keller, emergency coordinator for the WFP.
"A lot of people -- about 400,000 -- lost their food supply in the coming year," Keller told Reuters.
About 2,000 tonnes of rice had already been supplied for emergency food-for-work programmes, he said.
This land-locked nation has contended with floods in 1991, droughts in 1992 and 1993, and floods again in 1994 and 1995.
Agriculture accounts for 55 percent of economic activity in communist Laos, according to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
About 80 percent of the population works in agriculture, and 81 percent of the land under cultivation is used to grow rice.
Keller said that because of poor irrigation, most farmers could harvest only one crop of rice per year, compared with two or three in neighbouring countries.
The UNDP estimated that less than two percent of rice paddies were irrigated.
Flooding in 1996 caused 100 percent losses in the most productive areas of rice cultivation, in central and southern Laos.
The WFP estimated yields at between 0.9 and 1.2 tonnes per hectare in partially damaged areas and 1.8 to 2.25 tonnes per hectare in areas uneffected by floods.
